stimuli.text: A particle moves along the x-axis. Its velocity is given by $$v(t) = 4\sin\left(\frac{t^2}{3}\right) - 1$$ for $$0 \leq t \leq 4$$. At time $$t = 0$$ the particle is at position $$x = -2$$.
The curves $$r = 3 + 2\cos\theta$$ and $$r = 4$$ are drawn in the polar plane for $$0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi$$.
Consider the differential equation $$\frac{dy}{dx} = 2x(y + 2)$$. Let $$y = f(x)$$ be the particular solution with $$f(1) = -4$$.
A particle moves along the x-axis with velocity $$v(t) = 3t^{2} - 18t + 24$$ for $$t \geq 0$$. At time $$t = 0$$ the particle is at $$x = 3$$.
Consider the curve given by $$x^2 + xy + y^2 = 48$$.
A function $$f$$ has derivatives of all orders. Selected values are $$f(1) = 0$$, $$f'(1) = 1$$, $$f''(1) = -1$$ and $$f'''(1) = -3$$. For all $$x$$, $$|f^{(4)}(x)| \leq 18$$.

questions.stem: A particle moves in the plane with $$x'(t) = \frac{5}{3}t$$ and $$y'(t) = \frac{4}{3}t^2$$. What is the speed of the particle at $$t = 3$$?

options.why: This forgets the square root.
This is the slope of the path, not the speed.
Speed is the magnitude of the velocity vector, not the sum of its components.

questions.explanation: At $$t = 3$$, $$\vec{v} = \langle 5, 12 \rangle$$, so the speed is $$\sqrt{25 + 144} = 13$$.

questions.stem: Let $$f(x) = 2x^{3} - 3x^{2} - 12x$$. At what value of $$x$$ does $$f$$ have a relative maximum?

options.why: $$f(0) = 0$$, but $$f'(0)$$ is not zero, so this is not a critical point.
Correct. $$f'(x) = 6(x + 1)(x - 2)$$ changes from positive to negative at $$x = -1$$.
At this critical point $$f'$$ changes from negative to positive, which gives a relative minimum.
This is where f″ = 0 (the inflection point), not a critical point.

questions.explanation: $$f'(x) = 6x^2 - 6x - 12 = 6(x + 1)(x - 2)$$. Testing signs: $$f'$$ is positive left of $$-1$$, negative between $$-1$$ and $$2$$, positive right of $$2$$. So there is a relative maximum at $$-1$$ and a relative minimum at $$2$$.

questions.stem: If $$f(x) = \csc x$$, what is $$f'\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)$$?

options.why: This mixes up the derivative with a different trigonometric value at the point.
Check the sign: the derivatives of the co-functions (cot, csc) are negative; tan and sec are not.

This value doesn't come from the correct derivative formula.

questions.explanation: $$\frac{d}{dx}\left(\csc x\right) = -\csc x \cot x$$. Substituting $$x = \frac{\pi}{6}$$ gives $$-2\sqrt{3}$$.

questions.stem: If $$\int_0^{4} f(x)\,dx = 6$$ and $$\int_0^{6} f(x)\,dx = 11$$, what is $$\int_{4}^{6} \left(-2f(x) + 1\right)dx$$?

options.why: This adds the two given integrals; the integral from a to b is their difference.
Correct. $$\int_{4}^{6} f = 11 - (6) = 5$$, so the integral is $$-2(5) + 1(2)$$.
This forgets to multiply the integral of $$f$$ by $$-2$$.
The integral of the constant $$1$$ over an interval of length $$2$$ is $$2$$, not $$1$$.

questions.explanation: $$\int_{4}^{6} f(x)\,dx = \int_0^{6} f - \int_0^{4} f = 5$$. By linearity, the requested integral is $$-2 \cdot 5 + 1 \cdot 2 = -8$$.

questions.stem: Let $$f(x) = \begin{cases} -x - 3 & x < 3 \\ -2x + 2 & x \geq 3 \end{cases}$$. What is $$\lim_{x \to 3} f(x)$$?

options.why: Correct. The left-hand limit is $$-6$$ and the right-hand limit is $$-4$$. They differ, so the two-sided limit does not exist.

A limit is never the average of the one-sided limits. When they differ, the limit does not exist.
This is $$f(3)$$ and the right-hand limit only. The left-hand limit is $$-6$$.

questions.explanation: From the left, $$f(x) = -x - 3 \to -6$$. From the right, $$f(x) = -2x + 2 \to -4$$. Since $$-6 \neq -4$$, $$\lim_{x \to 3} f(x)$$ does not exist.

questions.stem: What is the sum of $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} 9\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)^n$$?

options.why: Correct. Geometric with first term $$-\frac{9}{2}$$ and ratio $$-\frac{1}{2}$$.

questions.stem: Using the line tangent to $$f(x) = \sqrt{x}$$ at $$x = 81$$, what is the approximation of $$\sqrt{83}$$?

questions.stem: The derivative of a function $$f$$ is $$f'(x) = (x + 1)^2(x - 1)$$. On which intervals is $$f$$ increasing?

options.why: The squared factor does not change sign at $$x = -1$$, so f′ < 0 for $$x < -1$$.
On $$-1 < x < 1$$ the factor $$x - 1$$ is negative.
Correct. The squared factor is never negative, so the sign of $$f'$$ matches $$x - 1$$.
Here f′ < 0 because $$x - 1 < 0$$.

questions.explanation: $$(x + 1)^2 \geq 0$$ for all $$x$$, so $$f'(x) > 0$$ exactly when $$x > 1$$. Note $$f'$$ does not change sign at $$-1$$, so there is no extremum there.

questions.stem: What is the coefficient of $$x^{4}$$ in the Maclaurin series for $$f(x) = e^{3x}$$?

questions.stem: What is $$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{e^{4x} - 1}{6x}$$?

options.why: Correct. The limit has the form $$\frac{0}{0}$$, so L'Hospital's Rule applies: $$\frac{4e^{4x}}{6}$$.

questions.stem: A function $$f$$ has $$f(-2) = -5$$, $$f'(-2) = 1$$, $$f''(-2) = -2$$ and $$f'''(-2) = 10$$. What is the coefficient of $$(x + 2)^3$$ in the Taylor polynomial for $$f$$ about $$x = -2$$?

questions.stem: The sum of $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n^{2}}$$ is approximated by its first 5 terms. What is the smallest upper bound on the error given by the alternating series error bound?

Which of the following series converge?

options.why: Correct. I: diverges (geometric with |r| = 5/4 ≥ 1). II: converges (absolute values form a p-series with p = 3). III: converges (p-series with p = 2 > 1).

Check each series with an appropriate test: I diverges, II converges, III converges.

questions.stem: What is the interval of convergence of $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(x - 3)^n}{n\cdot 6^n}$$?

options.why: Correct. Ratio test gives $$|x - 3| < 6$$; the left endpoint gives an alternating harmonic series (converges), the right endpoint the harmonic series (diverges).

questions.explanation: Ratio: $$\left|\frac{(x - 3)^{n+1}}{(n + 1)6^{n+1}}\cdot\frac{n\,6^n}{(x - 3)^n}\right| \to \frac{|x - 3|}{6}$$, so $$|x - 3| < 6$$. At $$x = 9$$: $$\sum \frac{1}{n}$$ diverges. At $$x = -3$$: $$\sum \frac{(-1)^n}{n}$$ converges.

parts.prompt: At what times in the interval $$0 < t < 4$$ does the particle change direction? Justify your answer.

rubric.criterion: Identifies the times where $$v$$ changes sign, with justification.
rubric.example: $$v(t)$$ changes sign at $$t \approx 0.871$$ and $$t \approx 2.944$$, so the particle changes direction there.

parts.prompt: Find the area of the region enclosed by $$r = 3 + 2\cos\theta$$.
Find the area of the region inside $$r = 3 + 2\cos\theta$$ and outside $$r = 4$$.

rubric.criterion: Writes outer squared minus inner squared.

parts.prompt: Find $$\frac{dr}{d\theta}$$ at $$\theta = 2$$. Is the curve moving toward or away from the origin at that angle? Explain.

rubric.example: Since $$r > 0$$ and $$\frac{dr}{d\theta} < 0$$, the curve is moving toward the origin.

parts.prompt: Find the slope of the line tangent to $$r = 3 + 2\cos\theta$$ at $$\theta = 2$$.
Find the slope of the slope-field segment at each of the points $$(-1, -1)$$, $$(0, 0)$$, $$(1, -3)$$ and $$(2, -2)$$.
Write an equation for the line tangent to the graph of $$f$$ at $$x = 1$$, and use it to approximate $$f(1.2)$$.

rubric.criterion: Finds the slope at the point and writes the tangent line.

parts.prompt: Find $$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$$ in terms of $$x$$ and $$y$$. Is the approximation in part (b) an overestimate or an underestimate? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Uses the sign of the second derivative at the point to conclude.
rubric.example: At $$(1, -4)$$, $$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = -12$$, so f is concave down and the tangent line lies above the curve: an overestimate.

parts.prompt: Find the particular solution $$y = f(x)$$ with $$f(1) = -4$$.
At what times does the particle change direction? Justify your answer.

rubric.criterion: Gives both times with a sign-change justification.

parts.prompt: Is the speed of the particle increasing or decreasing at time $$t = 0$$? Give a reason.

rubric.criterion: Finds the velocity and acceleration at the time.

rubric.example: Opposite signs, so the speed is decreasing.

parts.prompt: Find the position of the particle at time $$t = 6$$.

rubric.criterion: Uses the initial position and an antiderivative of $$v$$.

parts.prompt: Find the total distance traveled by the particle from $$t = 0$$ to $$t = 6$$.

rubric.criterion: Splits the motion at the turning points.

parts.prompt: Show that $$\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{2x + y}{x + 2y}$$.

rubric.criterion: Differentiates implicitly, using the product rule on the $$xy$$ term.
Solves for $$\frac{dy}{dx}$$ to reach the given expression.

parts.prompt: Write an equation for the line tangent to the curve at the point $$(4, 4)$$.

rubric.criterion: Finds the slope and writes the line.

parts.prompt: Find the coordinates of every point on the curve at which the tangent line is horizontal.

rubric.criterion: Sets the numerator equal to zero.
Substitutes into the curve and solves.

parts.prompt: Find $$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$$ at the point $$(4, 4)$$.

rubric.criterion: Differentiates $$\frac{dy}{dx}$$ with the quotient rule, treating $$y$$ as a function of $$x$$.

parts.prompt: Write the third-degree Taylor polynomial for $$f$$ about $$x = 1$$.

rubric.criterion: Uses the correct coefficients, including factorials.

parts.prompt: Use $$P_3$$ to approximate $$f(1.5)$$.
Use the Lagrange error bound to show that the approximation in part (b) differs from $$f(1.5)$$ by at most $$\frac{3}{64}$$.

rubric.criterion: Writes the Lagrange bound with the given M.

parts.prompt: Write the second-degree Taylor polynomial for $$f'$$ about $$x = 1$$.

rubric.criterion: Differentiates $$P_3$$ (or uses the derivative values directly).
